questions.q: What firewall access does a self-hosted integration runtime actually need?
options: Outbound access only, on port 443
An inbound port opened for Azure to connect in
Both inbound and outbound ports on 443
No firewall configuration is possible — self-hosted IRs bypass firewalls entirely
questions.explain: The self-hosted IR always initiates its own connections outbound over HTTPS (443); nothing needs to be opened for inbound traffic.

questions.q: Which side initiates the connection between the self-hosted IR and Azure?
options: The self-hosted IR machine always initiates outbound
Azure Data Factory always initiates inbound to the on-premises machine
Whichever side has lower latency initiates the connection
The connection is initiated simultaneously by both sides
questions.explain: The self-hosted IR calls out to Azure — it never accepts an inbound connection — which is exactly why no inbound firewall rule is required.

questions.q: What does the self-hosted IR need outbound access to, besides Azure Data Factory itself?
options: Azure Relay, the Microsoft Download Center, and Azure Key Vault
Every Azure service in the subscription, with no specific list
Only Azure Data Factory — nothing else is required
A third-party VPN provider
questions.explain: The self-hosted IR's outbound traffic goes to a small, well-known set of destinations: Data Factory, Azure Relay (control channel), the Download Center (updates), and Key Vault when used.

questions.q: How does a self-hosted IR handle a network that requires all outbound traffic to go through an internal proxy?
options: The Configuration Manager has a dedicated HTTP proxy settings screen
It cannot be configured to use a proxy at all
You must disable the corporate proxy for the IR machine specifically
Proxy support requires a separate paid Azure add-on
questions.explain: The Configuration Manager lets you choose direct access, the Windows system proxy, or a custom proxy with its own address, port, and credentials.

questions.q: Why is the self-hosted IR's outbound-only, small-destination-set traffic pattern useful in a security review?
options: It's easy to justify — no new inbound exposure, and a small, well-known, stable destination list
It isn't useful; security teams generally reject self-hosted IRs regardless
It matters only for compliance paperwork, not actual security posture
It eliminates the need for encrypted credentials entirely
questions.explain: No inbound ports, a small documented destination set, and standard HTTPS on 443 together make this pattern straightforward for a network admin to review and approve.
